name: Unani medicine

card.summary: A Greco-Arabic system of traditional medicine whose regimens, herbal preparations and skin and hair remedies are used in South Asia to care for health and appearance.
card.note: Some traditional preparations have been reported to be toxic; regulators call for safety monitoring.

quick.overview:
Unani medicine is a traditional system that grew out of Greek humoral medicine (Hippocrates, Galen) and was developed by physicians of the Islamic world such as al-Razi and Ibn Sina. It is practised mainly in South Asia, where it is a state-recognised system of medicine.

Practitioners treat the whole person by balancing the four humours and an individual temperament, using herbal and mineral remedies, diet, massage, cupping, leeching and other "regimenal" therapies. People who follow it use these for skin, hair and general vitality, and a small number of clinical trials of Unani formulations (for example in skin conditions) have been published.
quick.how: People usually consult a hakim (Unani practitioner) or use over-the-counter Unani products such as herbal ointments, oils and tonics. Treatment combines remedies with diet, exercise and regimens such as massage, fomentation, cupping or leech therapy. Results are described over weeks to months depending on the condition.
quick.risks: Reviews note that some medicines traditionally used by Unani practitioners are known to be poisonous, and WHO-linked pharmacovigilance efforts call for safety monitoring of herbal drugs. Leech therapy and cupping carry procedure-related complications such as infection. Unqualified practitioners are a concern raised by Indian medical bodies. Researchers describe the humoral theory as pseudoscientific, and trial evidence for most formulations is limited to small studies.

lead: Unani medicine (Unani Tibb) is a traditional system of medicine rooted in ancient Greek humoral theory, systematised in the Islamic Golden Age and carried to South Asia, where it remains an officially recognised system [1][2]. Its framework holds that health depends on the balance of four humours (blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile) and on each person's temperament [1].

In relation to looks, Unani practice includes skin, hair and general-wellbeing care: herbal ointments and oils, dietary guidance and "regimenal therapies" such as massage, cupping (hijama) and leech therapy [1][3]. Followers use these to improve skin condition, complexion and vitality, and Unani texts are also used as a source of cosmetic and skin remedies in India [4].

Published research consists mainly of small trials and reviews, including an open-label study of a topical formulation in atopic dermatitis and a randomized trial of Unani formulations in ringworm infection (dermatophytosis) [5][6]. Scholars and encyclopedic sources describe the underlying humoral theory as pseudoscientific, and call for safety monitoring of Unani drugs [1].

angle.text: Followers of Unani medicine use herbal ointments, oils and regimens such as massage and cupping with the aim of improving skin condition and vitality. A few small trials of Unani topical formulations in skin conditions have been published.

paras: Unani theory descends from Hippocrates (c. 460-380 BCE) and Galen, and holds that health reflects a balance of four humours: blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile [1]. Disease is understood as a derangement of temperament; a Unani review of hypothyroidism, for instance, maps its symptoms onto a "cold temperament" with excess phlegm [7].
Treatment is individualised and uses four broad modalities: herbal and mineral medicine, regimenal therapy (massage, exercise, cupping, fomentation), diet, and surgery [1][8].

During the 8th-9th centuries the Abbasid translation movement in Baghdad rendered Greek medical texts into Arabic. Al-Razi (c. 865-925) wrote clinical works, and Ibn Sina (980-1037) completed the Canon of Medicine in 1025, which formalised diagnostics and pharmacology [1][2].

Unani reached India by the 12th century and flourished under the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughal Empire [1]. Under British rule Western medicine was prioritised; Hakim Ajmal Khan used Tibbia College in Delhi to resist a proposed ban on indigenous medicine [1]. After independence India set up the Central Council for Research in Unani Medicine (1978), and the AYUSH ministry became a full ministry in 2014; India had 57 Unani colleges in 2022 [1].

Unani formularies include topical ointments (marham) and oils for skin conditions, and a review of ethnodermatological plants in India covers herbal skin treatments drawn from Ayurvedic and Unani traditions [4]. Regimens such as massage and cupping are used for pain and general wellbeing [8][9]. Leech therapy, known in Unani as part of regimenal therapy, is discussed in the medical literature for a range of conditions and has documented complications [10].

Studies of Unani practice are mostly small. An open-label interventional study examined the topical formulation Marham-e-Akbar in chronic atopic dermatitis [5]. A randomized controlled trial assessed Unani pharmacopoeial formulations in dermatophytosis [6]. Other randomized trials have examined Graeco-Arabic massage and hot medicated fomentation in low back pain, a polyherbal formulation in hypertensive heart disease, and a formulation for urinary stones [11][12][13][14]. Reviews summarise cupping for cervical spondylosis pain and leech therapy [8][10].

Encyclopedic sources describe Unani and humoral theory as pseudoscientific and note that some traditionally used medicines are poisonous; they cite WHO pharmacovigilance efforts calling for safety monitoring of herbal drugs, including Unani drugs [1]. The Indian Medical Association objects to unqualified practitioners who prescribe conventional medicines [1]. Leech therapy carries recognised complications [10].
